what: AAON makes heating and cooling equipment, mostly the large rooftop units that sit on top of commercial buildings. Through its BasX business it also builds custom cooling systems for data centres and cleanrooms, which is now the fastest-growing part of the company.
customers: Commercial building owners, contractors and engineers specifying HVAC for schools, offices, shops and industrial buildings, plus data centre developers buying custom liquid-cooling and air-handling systems.
money: Semi-custom rooftop units and air handlers for commercial buildings.
Custom data centre cooling, cleanroom systems and coils.
moat: AAON’s model is semi-custom manufacturing at near-standard cost: a customer can specify an unusual configuration and still get it from a production line rather than a workshop. That is hard to copy, it commands a price premium, and the engineers who specify these units tend to keep specifying them. In data centre cooling, the constraint is not demand but who can actually build the equipment, and BasX can.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $47.1M because capital spending of $213.3M exceeded operating cash flow of $166.2M. The company is spending more than it earns to build capacity.
The cash balance is effectively nil at $13,000, so that capacity is being funded from the revolver and from operating cash as it arrives.
The shares trade at about 31.5 times earnings for a company whose core business is tied to commercial construction.
Four analysts average a $117.50 target against $77.08. A 52% gap on four opinions is not a consensus and should not be treated as one.
Data centre cooling has attracted enormous investment from much larger competitors, so today’s capacity shortage is unlikely to last.
opportunities: Revenue has nearly tripled, from $534.5M in 2021 to $1.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.3B.
Data centre cooling demand per facility keeps rising because AI servers reject far more heat per rack than earlier hardware.
Debt is only $18.8M, so the capacity programme has not been financed with borrowings.
Commercial rooftop replacement demand is non-discretionary: when a unit fails, the building owner replaces it regardless of the economy.
watch: Whether capital spending peaks and cash flow turns positive while the data centre order book is still growing. Capacity that arrives after the shortage ends is the specific way this story goes wrong.
view: AAON has been one of the better-run mid-cap industrials in America for thirty years, and the market knows it: this has almost never been a cheap stock. What has changed is the reason to own it. For most of its history AAON was a steady compounder selling rooftop units into commercial construction, growing a little faster than the market because its semi-custom manufacturing let it charge more without costing more. Then it bought BasX, and found itself holding exactly the capability that data centre developers are desperate for. Revenue has gone from half a billion to well over two billion, and the multiple has gone along for the ride.

The thing to understand before paying 31 times earnings is that this is now a capital-spending story, not a margin story. Capital expenditure of $213 million exceeded operating cash flow of $166 million in the trailing year, the cash balance is essentially zero, and free cash flow is negative. None of that is alarming in itself — AAON is building plants because it has orders it cannot fill, which is the best reason a manufacturer ever has to spend money. But it changes the shape of the risk. A company funding expansion out of current cash flow has no cushion if orders slow mid-build, and it is spending into a market where Vertiv, Carrier and Trane are all expanding too. Capacity that lands after the shortage clears earns the industry’s normal return, not the current one.

I would also treat the single analyst target of $117.50 as noise rather than information. Four analysts on a $6.4 billion company tells you the stock is under-researched relative to its size, which is interesting, but a 52% implied upside from four opinions is a coin toss dressed as a forecast. The useful question is narrower: AAON’s core commercial business is a decent, cyclical, replacement-driven franchise probably worth something in the high teens to low twenties times earnings. Everything above that is the market capitalising BasX at a data-centre multiple. Whether that is right depends entirely on whether the data centre cooling business has a durable position or merely an early one.

My own read is that the core business justifies owning this through a cycle and the data centre piece is a genuine option rather than a certainty, which makes the current price fair rather than attractive. The moment that changes is when capital spending rolls over and the cash comes through: a company earning $200 million-plus of free cash flow on a growing data centre backlog is worth considerably more than one consuming cash to get there. That is the inflection to wait for, and it should be visible in the cash flow statement several quarters before it shows up in the earnings.
bull: The plants come online into a still-tight data centre cooling market, capital spending rolls over, and free cash flow arrives on a much larger revenue base.
bear: Capacity lands just as the big HVAC companies finish their own expansions, data centre cooling becomes an ordinary industrial market, and a 31 times multiple meets commercial-construction growth.
